title: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for heavy menstrual bleeding
condition_or_topic: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) in women of reproductive years
clinical_background: HMB can substantially impair physical and psychosocial well-being and is a common reason for seeking gynaecological care. Although research often defines it as menstrual blood loss of 80 mL or more per period, that volume is difficult to measure in clinical practice, where the woman's experience of bleeding also matters. Treatments include surgery and several medical options. NSAIDs are of interest because they inhibit cyclo-oxygenase and lower prostaglandin levels, which are elevated in women with excessive menstrual bleeding; they may also relieve dysmenorrhoea. Treatment choice involves effectiveness, tolerability, patient preference and contraceptive needs. NSAIDs are contraindicated when HMB occurs with an underlying bleeding disorder because they inhibit platelet aggregation.
objectives: Assess the effectiveness, safety and tolerability of NSAIDs for reducing menstrual blood loss in women of reproductive years with HMB.
Compare individual NSAIDs used for HMB to examine whether their effectiveness differs.
clinical_question: In women of reproductive years with regular HMB without pathological or treatment-induced causes, how do NSAIDs, alone or combined with another medical treatment, compare with placebo, other medical treatments or individual NSAIDs in reducing menstrual blood loss, and what are their safety and tolerability?
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled comparisons of NSAIDs, alone or combined with another medical treatment, against placebo, other medical treatments or another NSAID. Searches were updated in April 2019 across specialised registers, bibliographic databases, trial registries, conference sources and reference lists. Two review authors independently selected studies; three independently extracted data.

population.description: Women of reproductive age with regular heavy menstrual bleeding and no pathological or treatment-induced cause. The included studies enrolled 759 women.
inclusion_criteria: Regular heavy periods documented objectively as menstrual blood loss greater than 80 mL for one or more cycles before treatment, or reported subjectively by the woman.
Women of reproductive age recruited through primary care, family planning services or specialist clinics.
exclusion_criteria: Postmenopausal bleeding, described in the review criteria as less than one year from the last period.
Pathological causes of heavy menstrual bleeding.
Iatrogenic causes of heavy menstrual bleeding.
population.care_setting: Primary care, family planning services and specialist clinics.

interventions: NSAIDs at varying doses and by varying routes, including comparisons involving MFA, naproxen, ibuprofen, flurbiprofen, meclofenamic acid, diclofenac and acetylsalicylic acid.
NSAIDs combined with other medical treatment, including tranexamic acid plus mefenamic acid.
comparators: Other medical treatments, including tranexamic acid, ethamsylate, danazol, oral progestogens, progesterone-releasing intrauterine system, LNG IUS and OCP.

primary: Menstrual blood loss assessed objectively by the alkaline haematin method in mL/cycle, by PBAC score, or through the woman's reported perception of bleeding.
Change in quality of life recorded with a reproducible, validated method, including dysmenorrhoea and other menstrual symptoms.
secondary: TMFL measured from the change in weight of sanitary materials.
Number of bleeding days during the treatment cycle.

statistical_methods: Dichotomous outcomes were expressed as ORs with 95% CI and combined, where appropriate, using the Peto OR in Review Manager 5. Continuous outcomes were combined as MDs using post-treatment means and SDs or changes from baseline with their SDs. Meta-analysis required sufficient clinical and methodological similarity; unexplained substantial heterogeneity prompted a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using CI overlap, Chi2 tests with P < 0.10 as the threshold for significant heterogeneity, and I2. When approximately normally distributed data were reported only as medians and ranges, the median was treated as the mean and SD estimated as the range multiplied by 0.95/4, with sensitivity analyses. Highly skewed results were described separately. Analyses were per randomised woman where possible, without imputing missing values. Cross-over results generally were not pooled with parallel-group results when first-period data were unavailable.
follow_up: Treatment usually lasted two to three menstrual cycles; van Eijkeren 1992 used one month. Chamberlain 1991 included 1 cycle after treatment, Reid 2005 followed participants for 6 months, and Najam 2010 measured outcomes at 3 and 6 months.
quality_assessment_tool: Cochrane 'Risk of bias' assessment tool for individual studies; GRADE criteria for the overall quality of evidence for primary outcomes.
interpretation: The review finds limited evidence that NSAIDs, most often studied as mefenamic acid (MFA), reduce heavy menstrual bleeding more than placebo, although the benefit is modest and some women continue to have objectively excessive bleeding after treatment. tranexamic acid, danazol and the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG IUS) appear more effective at reducing blood loss. danazol also shortens bleeding but causes more adverse events than NSAIDs. Comparisons with ethamsylate, luteal-phase oral progestogen, the older progesterone-releasing intrauterine system and the oral contraceptive pill (OCP) do not establish clear differences in blood-loss reduction. Limited comparisons of MFA and naproxen show no clear efficacy difference; gastrointestinal adverse events were less likely with MFA in one small trial.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors found no earlier systematic review of NSAIDs. A cross-over trial by Andersch 1988 supported the analysed finding that tranexamic acid reduced menstrual blood loss more than an NSAID. The published Mann-Whitney U test in Hall 1987 agreed with the review's finding of no clear blood-loss difference between MFA and naproxen. Separately from the randomised evidence, Fraser 1983 followed 34 women receiving MFA over a 16-month period and reported sustained blood-loss reductions of 25% to 35% and improved quality of life. The authors also describe NICE 2007 guidance as recommending NSAIDs alongside tranexamic acid and OCPs as second-line options when hormonal or non-hormonal treatment is acceptable, and alongside tranexamic acid as a first-line option when hormonal treatment is unacceptable.
clinical_implications: The demonstrated blood-loss reduction with NSAIDs is modest; treatment may leave some women with objectively excessive bleeding.

A convincing history of heavy bleeding does not necessarily correspond to excessive loss measured by the alkaline haematin method. The authors consider blood-loss-reducing treatment less likely to work as well for women whose measured loss is not excessive.
The older progesterone-releasing intrauterine system was withdrawn from the market in 2001 and should be distinguished from the LNG IUS when interpreting comparisons.
In the short term, abdominal pain was more likely with LNG IUS than MFA; the authors note that this effect generally resolved over time.
The review states that NSAIDs are contraindicated when heavy menstrual bleeding coexists with an underlying bleeding disorder because they inhibit platelet aggregation.
practice_implications: When choosing medical treatment, account for the woman's preferences and contraceptive needs as well as each option's benefits and risks.
Evaluate treatment using more than blood-loss efficacy alone: the authors also identify cost, convenience, beneficial effects on symptoms and adverse effects as relevant.
The authors state that danazol is not a usual or recommended treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding, despite its greater blood-loss reduction in the reviewed trials.
limitations: The 19 included trials were small and underpowered; many outcomes and comparisons depended on only one trial.
Evidence quality ranged from low to moderate, principally because of risk of bias, inadequately reported study methods and imprecision associated with small studies.

Only nine trials contributed data to meta-analyses. Cross-over data often could not be pooled, one trial had highly skewed data, another lacked variance measures, and an included trial had no comparison data available.
The sole placebo-controlled trial in the blood-loss meta-analysis was not high quality: 42% of randomised participants dropped out, and its analysis was not intention to treat.

Cameron 1987 and Chamberlain 1991 had treatment groups that were not comparable at baseline. The authors particularly caution that pretreatment blood loss in the danazol group of Cameron 1987 was significantly higher than in its other groups.
The comparison with the older progesterone-releasing intrauterine system came from a very small study whose baseline imbalance may have affected its results.
For some trials, positively skewed blood-loss data required substituting a median for a mean and estimating an SD for meta-analysis. Sensitivity analyses did not substantially change the findings.

Trials generally examined only two or three menstrual cycles of treatment. Randomised evidence did not establish longer-term effects, and the included comparisons did not adequately assess longer oral progestogen regimens.
Several outcomes were insufficiently assessed, particularly dysmenorrhoea, adherence, acceptability and adverse events. No included trial provided data on the cost or resource use of NSAID treatment.
The comprehensive search reduced the possibility of publication bias but could not exclude it; too few studies were available for a meaningful funnel-plot analysis.
Some participants reported heavy bleeding despite having normal measured blood loss, which the authors consider likely to have underestimated some treatment–placebo differences.
strengths: The authors used a comprehensive study search and methods for study selection, data extraction and quality assessment intended to minimise review-author error and bias.
Sensitivity analyses indicated that including trials with non-comparable groups at baseline did not substantially alter the meta-analysis results.
open_questions: Whether women seeking care for unacceptable menstrual loss are more concerned with its total volume than with its blood content remains to be established.
Whether adding NSAIDs to another medical treatment improves efficacy remains uncertain.
Comparative efficacy and adverse-event differences among individual NSAIDs have not been thoroughly investigated in randomised studies.
future_directions: Conduct further RCTs comparing individual NSAIDs to identify the best treatment option.
In future heavy-menstrual-bleeding treatment comparisons, consider longer treatment across multiple cycles and an oral progestogen regimen given during three of the four weeks of the cycle.
Use adequately designed trials to investigate whether adding NSAIDs to other medical treatments improves efficacy.
Further assess dysmenorrhoea, treatment adherence and acceptability, and adverse events, which the existing comparisons evaluated inadequately.

main_findings.description: In van Eijkeren 1992, menstrual blood loss was lower with mefenamic acid than with placebo.
main_findings.context: 1 study; 11 women. Post-treatment mean (SD): mefenamic acid 65 (19) mL, n = 6; placebo 189 (69) mL, n = 5. The review rated the evidence Low.

main_findings.description: In Grover 1990, fewer women reported no subjective relief of heavy menstrual bleeding with mefenamic acid than with placebo.
main_findings.context: 1 study; 80 women. The study did not explain how relief was assessed; the review rated the evidence Low.

main_findings.description: In five of seven post-treatment comparisons from cross-over trials, mean menstrual blood loss differed in favour of NSAIDs versus placebo; the comparisons of low-dose ibuprofen and of mefenamic acid in Muggeridge 1983 did not show a clear difference.
main_findings.context: These cross-over results were described separately rather than pooled.

main_findings.description: In Fraser 1981, mean menstrual blood loss in the ovulatory menorrhagia subgroup was lower during mefenamic acid cycles than during placebo cycles.
main_findings.context: n = 28; paired t test, t = 6.56; cross-over result not pooled.

main_findings.context: n = 15; Wilcoxon Sum Rank Test; cross-over result not pooled.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: The review did not calculate a single adverse-event rate across treatments. In van Eijkeren 1992, adverse events occurred in 2/6 women receiving mefenamic acid and 2/5 receiving placebo (Peto OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.07 to 8.09; P=0.83). In Dockeray 1989, they occurred in 6/20 receiving MFA and 15/20 receiving danazol (Peto OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.59; P=0). In Cameron 1990, total adverse events occurred in 10/17 receiving NSAIDs and 11/15 receiving oral progestogens, without a clear difference (Peto OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.13 to 2.26; P=0.4). In Hall 1987, total adverse events occurred in 15/17 receiving mefenamic acid and 18/18 receiving naproxen, without a clear difference (Peto OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.00; P=0.14).
safety_results.discontinuations: In Reid 2005, MFA was discontinued by 4 women: 1 for non-compliance, 2 for diarrhoea and 1 for ineffective treatment; LNG IUS was discontinued by 4 women: 2 after partial expulsion and 2 after full expulsion. In Dockeray 1989, 1 woman in the MFA group withdrew because of adverse effects. In van Eijkeren 1992, 1 woman discontinued MFA because of rash and itching.
notable_adverse_events: Hall 1987: gastrointestinal events occurred in 6/17 women receiving mefenamic acid and 13/18 receiving naproxen; the difference favoured mefenamic acid (Peto OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.87; P=0.03). Central nervous system events occurred in 6/17 and 5/18, respectively, without a clear difference (Peto OR 1.40, 95% CI 0.34 to 5.73; P=0.64).

Cameron 1990, NSAIDs versus oral progestogens: headache 4/17 versus 5/15 (Peto OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.14 to 2.86; P=0.54); abdominal pain 3/17 versus 3/15 (Peto OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.15 to 4.96; P=0.87); nausea 2/17 versus 1/15 (Peto OR 1.79, 95% CI 0.17 to 18.65; P=0.63). None showed a clear difference.

Reid 2005, NSAIDs versus LNG IUS: headache 10/26 versus 10/25 (Peto OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.31 to 2.86; P=0.91); abdominal pain 2/26 versus 8/25 (Peto OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.87; P=0.03); ovarian cyst 3/26 versus 6/25 (Peto OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.80; P=0.25); breast pain 2/26 versus 6/25 (Peto OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.33; P=0.11). Only abdominal pain showed a clear difference, favouring NSAIDs.

Reid 2005, NSAIDs versus LNG IUS: nausea 4/26 versus 2/25 (Peto OR 2.01, 95% CI 0.37 to 10.86; P=0.42); diarrhoea 4/26 versus 1/25 (Peto OR 3.53, 95% CI 0.57 to 21.98; P=0.18); upper respiratory infection 5/26 versus 5/25 (Peto OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.24 to 3.75; P=0.95). None showed a clear difference.
Andersch 1988 reported adverse effects in 47% of women during tranexamic acid treatment and 27% during flurbiprofen treatment; the difference was not tested.
Ylikorkala 1986 reported adverse effects in 7% of women during placebo treatment and 0% during naproxen treatment; the difference was not tested.
Muggeridge 1983 reported nausea as the reason for withdrawal of 1 woman; the treatment during which it occurred was not specified.

subgroup_analyses: The review compared individual NSAIDs with placebo and assessed their adverse events separately. In Makarainen 1986, the comparison favoured ibuprofen 1200 mg daily over placebo for menstrual blood loss (P < 0.01), whereas the review found no clear difference for ibuprofen 600 mg daily.

Fraser 1981 reported results for the subgroup with ovulatory menorrhagia (n = 28), rather than pooling results across participants with different causes of bleeding. Its subgroup comparison favoured mefenamic acid over placebo for menstrual blood loss (P < 0.001).

Sensitivity analyses excluding Cameron 1987, whose treatment groups differed at baseline, did not change the review's conclusions substantially. Analyses with and without studies for which means and SDs were estimated were used to assess that assumption; few studies per outcome restricted other planned sensitivity analyses.
secondary_results: Bonnar 1996, NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid: days of bleeding did not clearly differ (Mean Difference (IV, Fixed, 95% CI) 0.40 days [-0.47, 1.27]; 49 women; P=0.37). Mean (SD) duration was 5.3 (1.3) days with NSAIDs, n = 23, and 4.9 (1.8) days with tranexamic acid, n = 26.

Across Cameron 1987 and Dockeray 1989, menstrual bleeding lasted longer with NSAIDs than with danazol (Mean Difference (IV, Fixed, 95% CI) 1.03 days [0.26, 1.80]; 53 women; 2 studies; I² = 0%; P=0.01). The review rated this evidence Moderate.

Cameron 1987, NSAIDs versus danazol: mean (SD) bleeding duration was 5 (0.7) versus 4 (1) days (Mean Difference 1 [0.06, 1.94]; n = 8 versus n = 6). Dockeray 1989: corresponding means (SD) were 5.9 (1.1) versus 4.8 (2.9) days (Mean Difference 1.1 [-0.26, 2.46]; n = 19 versus n = 20).

Across Cameron 1987 and Cameron 1990, days of bleeding did not clearly differ between NSAIDs and oral progestogens (Mean Difference (IV, Fixed, 95% CI) -0.41 days [-0.95, 0.13]; 48 women; 2 studies; I² = 35.2%; P=0.14). The review rated this evidence Moderate.

Cameron 1987, NSAIDs versus oral progestogens: mean (SD) duration was 5 (0.7) versus 5 (1) days (Mean Difference 0 [-0.85, 0.85]; n = 8 per group). Cameron 1990: mean (SD) duration was 5.4 (0.9) versus 6.1 (1.1) days (Mean Difference -0.7 [-1.41, 0.01]; n = 17 versus n = 15).
Cameron 1990, NSAIDs versus oral progestogens: non-adherence occurred in 1/17 versus 1/15 women; there was no clear difference (Peto OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.05 to 14.78; 32 women; P=0.93).

Cameron 1987: bleeding duration was shorter with NSAIDs than with the older progesterone-releasing IUS (Mean Difference (IV, Fixed, 95% CI) -5.00 days [-6.08, -3.92]; 16 women; P<0.0001). Mean (SD) duration was 5 (0.7) days with NSAIDs and 10 (1.4) days with the IUS, with n = 8 per group. The review rated this evidence Low.

Hall 1987: bleeding duration did not clearly differ between mefenamic acid and naproxen (Mean Difference (IV, Fixed, 95% CI) -0.40 days [-1.59, 0.79]; 35 women; P=0.51). Mean (SD) duration was 6 (1.8) days with mefenamic acid, n = 17, and 6.4 (1.8) days with naproxen, n = 18.

For the comparisons assessed, the review found no randomised-trial data suitable for meta-analysis of treatment costs or resource use. Jaisamrarn 2006 contributed no outcome data to comparative analyses.
