main_conclusion: NSAIDs reduce heavy menstrual bleeding compared with placebo, but tranexamic acid, danazol and LNG IUS reduce bleeding more effectively. Evidence does not establish a clear efficacy difference between NSAIDs and several other medical treatments; danazol causes more adverse events, and the comparisons are constrained by small studies.
narrative_summary: This Cochrane review assessed the effectiveness, safety and tolerability of NSAIDs for heavy menstrual bleeding in women of reproductive age. It included 19 randomised trials involving 759 women; data from nine trials were suitable for meta-analysis. Compared with placebo, mefenamic acid reduced measured menstrual blood loss by -124.0 mL/cycle (95% CI -186.36 to -61.64; 11 participants in 1 study), while the odds of reporting no subjective improvement were lower (Peto OR 0.08 [0.03, 0.18]; 80 participants in 1 study). Tranexamic acid and danazol reduced blood loss more than NSAIDs. In the danazol comparison, the mean difference was 45.06 mL/cycle (95% CI 18.73 to 71.39; 79 women; 3 studies), but adverse events were less frequent with mefenamic acid (Peto OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.59; 40 women). LNG IUS was also more effective than NSAIDs in the authors’ overall assessment. Comparisons with ethamsylate, luteal-phase oral progestogens, the older progesterone-releasing intrauterine system and the oral contraceptive pill did not establish clear efficacy differences. Mefenamic acid and naproxen showed no clear difference in blood-loss reduction, although gastrointestinal adverse events favoured mefenamic acid in one small study. Evidence quality ranged from low to moderate, principally because of bias and imprecision. The authors emphasise that treatment assessment also involves acceptability, symptoms and adverse effects, and that the available trials offer limited evidence about longer-term outcomes.

document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: The abstract outlines the rationale, objective, methods, findings, and conclusions of the review; these are detailed in its subsections.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) substantially affects the health of premenopausal women. Medical treatments offer alternatives to surgery. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) lower prostaglandin levels, which are elevated with excessive menstrual bleeding, and may also ease dysmenorrhoea.

document_sections.heading: Objectives
document_sections.content: The review aimed to assess whether NSAIDs reduce menstrual blood loss (MBL) in women of reproductive age with HMB, and to evaluate their safety and tolerability.

document_sections.heading: Search methods
document_sections.content: In April 2019, the authors searched the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility specialised register, Cochrane Central Register of Studies Online (CENTRAL CRSO), MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, trial registries, and article reference lists.

document_sections.heading: Selection criteria
document_sections.content: Eligible studies randomly compared individual NSAIDs, or NSAIDs combined with another medical treatment, against another NSAID, placebo, or a medical treatment. Participants had regular heavy periods assessed objectively or subjectively, without a pathological or treatment-induced cause.

document_sections.heading: Data collection and analysis
document_sections.content: The review included 19 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving 759 women. Two authors independently extracted data. Data from nine trials supported estimates of odds ratios (ORs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes. Results were presented descriptively for seven cross-over trials unsuitable for pooling, one trial with skewed data, and one trial without variance measures. Another trial supplied no analysable data.

document_sections.heading: Main results
document_sections.content: Overall, NSAIDs reduced HMB more effectively than placebo but less effectively than tranexamic acid, danazol, or the levonorgestrelreleasing intrauterine system (LNG IUS). Compared with NSAIDs, danazol shortened menstruation but caused more adverse events; the trials informing this comparison dated from 1980 to 1990, and treatment acceptability did not appear to differ. Danazol is currently neither usual nor recommended for HMB. No clear difference was established against oral luteal progestogen, ethamsylate, an older progesterone-releasing intrauterine system, or the oral contraceptive pill (OCP); most studies lacked adequate power. Evidence did not show a difference between naproxen and mefenamic acid for reducing HMB. Evidence quality ranged from low to moderate, chiefly because of bias risk and imprecision.

document_sections.heading: Authors' conclusions
document_sections.content: NSAIDs reduce HMB relative to placebo, but tranexamic acid, danazol, and LNG IUS are more effective. Adverse events are more severe with danazol. The few small evaluable studies did not establish a clear efficacy difference between NSAIDs and oral luteal progestogen, ethamsylate, OCP, or the older progesterone-releasing intrauterine system.

document_sections.heading: P L A I N L A N G U A G E S U M M A R Y
document_sections.content: This summary addresses the effectiveness and safety of NSAIDs for HMB before menopause; its clinical findings and evidence-quality assessment appear in the subsections below.

document_sections.heading: Review question
document_sections.content: The authors examined whether NSAIDs help reduce HMB in women who have not reached menopause.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Prostaglandin levels are raised in women with excessive menstrual bleeding and lowered by NSAIDs. This provided a reason to investigate possible benefits for heavy bleeding and painful periods.

document_sections.heading: Study characteristics
document_sections.content: The database search identified 19 eligible RCTs involving 759 women. Only nine trials provided data suitable for analysis.

document_sections.heading: Key results
document_sections.content: Women sought care when HMB impaired quality of life. NSAIDs modestly reduced HMB, while danazol, tranexamic acid, and LNG IUS were more effective. These findings rested on a small number of trials of low to moderate quality.

document_sections.heading: Quality of the evidence
document_sections.content: Evidence quality ranged from low to moderate. Inadequate reporting of study methods and imprecision arising from small numbers of studies were the principal problems.

document_sections.heading: S U M M A R Y O F F I N D I N G S
document_sections.content: The summary tables display comparative MBL, perceived improvement, bleeding duration, and quality-of-life outcomes for NSAIDs against placebo and other treatments, and for mefenamic acid against naproxen. They provide participant and study counts, effect estimates, comparative risks where applicable, and GRADE ratings. The tables state when an outcome was not reported. Their footnotes explain that assumed comparison-group risk underlies corresponding intervention-group risk and describe downgrading for imprecision, bias risk, or heterogeneity.

document_sections.heading: B A C K G R O U N D Description of the condition
document_sections.content: HMB, also termed menorrhagia, is a common gynaecological problem that harms health and quality of life and uses substantial healthcare resources. In the UK, one in 20 women aged 30 to 49 years consult a doctor for HMB each year (NICE 2018); a European study found symptoms during the preceding 12 months in 27% of women of reproductive age (Fraser 2014). Research has often defined HMB as MBL of 80 mL or more per period without pregnancy or a known pelvic or systemic disease, but this volume is difficult to quantify clinically. Women usually judge bleeding to be unacceptable when its quantity or frequency disrupts physical or psychosocial well-being; that judgment commonly drives treatment and assessment of its effect. The International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) defined HMB from the woman's perspective of increased menstrual volume, irrespective of cycle regularity, frequency, or duration (Munro 2011). Studies have commonly measured blood loss with alkaline haematin; the pictorial blood loss assessment chart (PBAC) provides a simpler method based on scores assigned to used sanitary products. Total menstrual fluid loss (TMFL), determined from the change in pad or tampon weight, has also been proposed: it correlates with changes in objectively measured MBL and may matter particularly to women concerned about flooding. Although surgery has traditionally been prominent, 80% of surgically treated women have no anatomical pathology, and over a third of hysterectomies for excessive bleeding remove a normal uterus (Clarke 1995; Gath 1982). Medical therapy can therefore avoid potentially unnecessary surgery and preserve fertility.

document_sections.heading: Description of the intervention
document_sections.content: Available medicines for HMB include hormonal treatments, antifibrinolytics, and NSAIDs; their effectiveness, tolerability, and acceptability differ. Treatment choice should account for patient preference, contraceptive needs, benefits, and risks. NSAIDs are considered useful when contraception is not desired, particularly with dysmenorrhoea (Fraser 2008). NSAIDs listed for HMB are mefenamic acid (MFA), naproxen, ibuprofen, flurbiprofen, meclofenamic acid, diclofenac, indomethacin, and acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin).

document_sections.heading: How the intervention might work
document_sections.content: Evidence implicating prostaglandins in HMB supports investigation of NSAIDs. Compared with normal menses, excessive bleeding is associated with higher endometrial prostaglandin E2 and prostaglandin F2α. Elevated ratios of prostaglandin E2 to F2α and of prostacyclin (prostaglandin I2) to thromboxane A2 offer further evidence of disturbed haemostasis. These substances occur in both endometrium and myometrium, but how they produce excessive blood loss remains speculative. NSAIDs inhibit the cyclo-oxygenase enzyme and thereby lower prostaglandin levels. Because they inhibit platelet aggregation, NSAIDs are contraindicated in women who have both HMB and an underlying bleeding disorder.

document_sections.heading: Why it is important to do this review
document_sections.content: Roy 2004 reported MBL reductions of 25% to 35% or more in about three-quarters of women with HMB treated with NSAIDs. These drugs may also improve associated dysmenorrhoea. Adverse effects, particularly gastrointestinal ones, vary in frequency but are usually not severe. Comparing this option with other treatments in effectiveness, tolerability, acceptability, and safety can support informed choice. Because individual responses may differ despite an assumption of similar efficacy among NSAIDs, the review also compared individual agents.

document_sections.heading: O B J E C T I V E S
document_sections.content: The authors sought to establish the effectiveness, safety, and tolerability of NSAIDs for reducing MBL in women of reproductive age with HMB.

document_sections.heading: M E T H O D S Criteria for considering studies for this review
document_sections.content: The review prespecified eligible study designs, participants, interventions, and outcomes, as detailed below.

document_sections.heading: Types of studies
document_sections.content: Eligible studies randomly compared an NSAID, alone or alongside another medical therapy, with placebo or another medical therapy for HMB. Direct comparisons between NSAIDs were also eligible.

document_sections.heading: Types of participants Inclusion criteria
document_sections.content: Eligible participants were women of reproductive age with regular heavy periods, recruited in primary care, family planning, or specialist clinics. Heavy bleeding could be established objectively as greater than 80 mL for one or more cycles before intervention or reported subjectively. The preceding-cycle requirement changed from two or more to one or more cycles in the 2007 and 2012 updates. Exclusions comprised postmenopausal bleeding described here as less than one year from the last period, irregular or intermenstrual bleeding, and pathological or iatrogenic causes of HMB.

document_sections.heading: Types of interventions
document_sections.content: The review considered NSAIDs against placebo or other medicines, including antifibrinolytics, hormonal treatment, danazol, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues; comparisons among MFA, naproxen, ibuprofen, flurbiprofen, meclofenamic acid, diclofenac, and acetylsalicylic acid; and NSAIDs added to other medical treatments against those treatments without an NSAID. The combination comparison was introduced in the 2012 update. Doses and administration routes were not restricted.

document_sections.heading: Types of outcome measures
document_sections.content: Available primary outcomes were MBL assessed objectively by alkaline haematin in mL/cycle, subjectively with a PBAC score or patient report, and change in quality of life measured reproducibly with a validated format. Quality-of-life assessment could include changes in dysmenorrhoea, headache, diarrhoea, depression, and other menstrual symptoms. Secondary outcomes were TMFL measured from sanitary-product weight change; days of bleeding during the treated cycle; adherence; treatment acceptability; adverse events of any severity, whether volunteered or elicited; and resource use or cost.

document_sections.heading: Searching other resources
document_sections.content: The authors also searched reference lists of relevant publications and identified trials.

document_sections.heading: Data collection and analysis
document_sections.content: Prespecified procedures governed study selection, data extraction, bias assessment, effect estimation, synthesis, and assessment of evidence quality.

document_sections.heading: Selection of studies
document_sections.content: Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts against prespecified eligibility criteria and independently assessed full texts when needed. They had planned to settle disagreements through discussion and consensus, but none arose.

document_sections.heading: Data extraction and management
document_sections.content: The authors examined randomisation, blinding, allocation concealment, numbers randomised or subsequently excluded or lost, intention-to-treat analysis, and power calculations. They recorded study duration, timing, and location; participant age, characteristics, eligibility criteria, and definitions of heavy MBL; treatment type, dose, and schedule; and methods of assessing MBL, satisfaction, symptoms, and quality of life. All three review authors independently extracted data with forms based on Cochrane guidance. They requested methodological or numerical details from investigators when necessary and extracted values from graphs when numerical results were unavailable. Analyses used the randomised woman as the unit. Data were analysed by intention to treat where possible; missing values were not imputed.

document_sections.heading: Search methods for identification of studies
document_sections.content: The original search took place in 1998, with updates in September/October 2001, April 2004, July 2007, July 2012, and April 2019.

document_sections.heading: Electronic searches
document_sections.content: On 1 April 2019, searches covered the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Specialised Register of Controlled Trials, CENTRAL CRSO, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, trial registries, conference abstracts, LILACS, clinical-study-results sources, PubMed, OpenSIGLE, GOOGLE, and GOOGLE Scholar. The stated database coverage began in 1946 for MEDLINE, 1980 for Embase, and 1806 for PsycINFO.

document_sections.heading: Dealing with missing data
document_sections.content: The authors used intention-to-treat data when available, sought missing information from study investigators, and did not substitute values when those attempts failed.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of risk of bias in included studies
document_sections.content: Two authors independently applied the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' assessment tool to sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcomes, and other bias, rating each domain low, unclear, or high risk. Disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third author.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of heterogeneity
document_sections.content: Before pooling, the authors considered clinical and methodological comparability. They examined dispersion, CI overlap, and outliers, used Chi2 with P < 0.10 as evidence of significant heterogeneity, and quantified heterogeneity using I2.

document_sections.heading: Measures of treatment effect
document_sections.content: Dichotomous outcomes were expressed as ORs with 95% CIs and pooled using the Peto OR in Review Manager 5. Continuous outcomes were combined as MDs using post-treatment means and standard deviations (SD), or baseline-to-final changes with their SD. When only medians and ranges were available and approximate normality was plausible, the median was treated as the mean and SD estimated as range multiplied by 0.95/4; sensitivity analyses tested this assumption. Strongly skewed results from small samples were not pooled. Higher values represented worse outcomes, so effects on the left of the plots favoured NSAIDs.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of reporting biases
document_sections.content: A broad search sought to limit publication bias. Too few studies were available for a funnel plot to provide a meaningful assessment of small-study effects.

document_sections.heading: Data synthesis
document_sections.content: Meta-analysis was undertaken when populations, treatments, outcomes, duration, and data format permitted a meaningful combination. Unexplained substantial heterogeneity prompted a random-effects model. Cross-over studies generally could not be combined with parallel-group studies because of possible carryover and differences in standard errors. The authors sought first-period cross-over data for a parallel-group comparison, but usually could not obtain them; remaining results were described separately.

document_sections.heading: Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity
document_sections.content: Subgroup analyses compared individual NSAIDs against placebo for efficacy and adverse events. The authors noted that pharmacological differences among NSAIDs are small, while individual responses and adverse-event patterns vary considerably.

document_sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
document_sections.content: Planned analyses examined differences in participants, treatments, outcomes, and adequate allocation concealment. Small study numbers per outcome restricted what could be undertaken.

document_sections.heading: Overall quality of the body of evidence; 'Summary of findings' tables
document_sections.content: The authors used GRADEpro GDT to prepare outcome summaries for MBL and quality of life. Two authors independently judged study limitations, consistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias using GRADE. Concerns for a criterion could lower the rating by one or two levels; overall ratings were high, moderate, low, or very low.

document_sections.heading: R E S U L T S Description of studies
document_sections.content: The following subsections describe the search, included and excluded studies, risk of bias, and treatment comparisons.

document_sections.heading: Results of the search
document_sections.content: The search found 25 RCTs of NSAID treatment for regular HMB; 19 met the review's inclusion criteria.

document_sections.heading: Included studies
document_sections.content: The included studies enrolled 759 women, although outcome-specific analyses used fewer participants because of multiple comparison groups. Jaisamrarn 2006 entered the review in the 2019 update without data usable for comparisons. Thirteen studies were conducted in Europe: six in the UK, two each in Ireland, Finland, and Sweden, and one in the Netherlands. Two took place in India, two in Australia, one in Thailand, and one in Canada. Most interventions lasted two to three menstrual cycles; treatment in van Eijkeren 1992 lasted only one month. The intrauterine systems remained in place throughout their trials, while OCP was taken during three of the four weeks of a cycle.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes
document_sections.content: All but two trials principally measured MBL objectively with alkaline haematin. Grover 1990 assessed the proportion reporting relief of HMB without explaining its measurement; Najam 2010 used PBAC. One trial also measured TMFL and PBAC. Five trials assessed bleeding days, eight adverse-event incidence, three dysmenorrhoea, two acceptability and perceived MBL change, and one non-adherence. Studies differed in how adverse events were elicited and reported: any event, specific events, or broad categories.

document_sections.heading: Trials included in the meta-analysis
document_sections.content: Meta-analyses used data from nine trials involving 419 women. Comparisons involved MFA against placebo, naproxen, danazol, tranexamic acid, ethamsylate, OCP, luteal-phase norethisterone, or the progesterone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS).

document_sections.heading: Participants
document_sections.content: In 18 included trials, ages ranged from 18 to 55 years; all participants had sought assistance for HMB. One trial enrolled women aged 12 to 45 years, of whom 67% were over 30 years. Ten studies required objectively defined HMB measured by alkaline haematin. Some required regular ovulatory cycles. Common exclusions were hormonal contraception, IUD use, fibroids, and pelvic pathology.

document_sections.heading: Data considered unsuitable for pooling in the meta-analysis (cross-over trials, trials with skewed data or no measure of variance)
document_sections.content: Seven cross-over trials involving 99 women supplied results unsuitable for pooling. Three compared MFA with placebo, two naproxen with placebo, one ibuprofen with placebo, and one flurbiprofen with tranexamic acid. Reid 2005 had markedly skewed results, and Najam 2010 supplied no variance measures; their results were therefore presented descriptively.

document_sections.heading: Interventions
document_sections.content: MFA was studied most often, generally at 500 mg three times a day from the onset of menstruation for four or five days or until bleeding stopped. Two studies began MFA four or five days before menstruation; Tsang 1987 used 500 mg initially followed by 250 mg four times per day for three to five days. Naproxen schedules differed among four studies: one began with 500 mg at onset and again three to five hours later, then 500 mg twice a day for five days; another used 500 mg in the morning and 250 mg in the afternoon on days one to two, followed by 250 mg twice a day for up to seven days; a third used 500 mg followed by 250 mg three to four times daily; and another used 550 mg initially followed by 275 mg four times daily for five days. The ibuprofen comparison tested 600 mg daily and 1200 mg daily against placebo. Tranexamic acid and ethamsylate were given during five days of menstruation, while danazol was administered daily throughout the cycle.

document_sections.heading: Excluded studies
document_sections.content: Martinez Alcala 1979 was excluded because its sanitary-pad-use outcome was an unreliable substitute for objectively measured MBL. Vargyas 1987 included seven women (21%) with IUDs, an excluded treatment-induced cause of bleeding. In the 2019 version, Gupta 2013 and Famuyide 2017 were excluded because randomisation was to broad treatment choices and participants could select a medical treatment that included NSAIDs. Naafe 2018 compared MFA against MFA plus herbal medicine and was excluded.

document_sections.heading: Risk of bias in included studies
document_sections.content: Study-level assessments covered randomisation, concealment, blinding, incomplete data, and other potential bias. Limitations included poorly reported procedures, withdrawals, and imbalances between treatment groups.

document_sections.heading: Allocation Sequence generation and allocation concealment
document_sections.content: Eight studies reported an adequate randomisation method and were rated low risk for sequence generation; 11 did not explain their method and were rated unclear. Only two of the 19 trials, van Eijkeren 1992 and Reid 2005, were rated low risk for allocation concealment. van Eijkeren 1992 was very small, had many withdrawals, and treated for only one month. Concealment risk was unclear in the remaining trials because adequate safeguards were not documented.

document_sections.heading: Blinding
document_sections.content: Ten of 19 studies were double-blind and rated low risk. One single-blind trial did not identify who was blinded and was rated unclear. The other studies did not report blinding; the authors considered it unlikely and rated them high risk.

document_sections.heading: Incomplete outcome data
document_sections.content: Nine of 19 trials did not clarify post-randomisation losses, exclusions, or withdrawals. Among the other 10, three reported loss to follow-up of 16% to 29%, while seven reported post-randomisation exclusions or withdrawals of 3% to 42%. Two trials with exclusions or withdrawals used intention-to-treat analysis and were regarded as low risk for this domain.

document_sections.heading: Other potential sources of bias
document_sections.content: Rybo 1981 reported findings for four women with primary menorrhagia from 14 randomised participants. Fraser 1981 enrolled women with varied diagnoses; its ovulatory-menorrhagia subgroup included a substantial proportion without objectively excessive bleeding and supplied no other subgroup outcomes. Two trials had confusing outcome data and were rated high risk for other bias; 14 supplied insufficient information and were rated unclear; three reported comparable baseline data and were rated low risk.

document_sections.heading: 1 NSAIDs versus placebo
document_sections.content: The review compared NSAIDs with placebo for blood loss, adverse events, and other outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective, subjective or both)
document_sections.content: Eight trials assessed MBL by differing methods. In one trial involving 11 women, MFA lowered mean MBL relative to placebo by MD –124 mL/cycle, 95% CI –186 to –62. Six cross-over trials could not be pooled; five of seven post-treatment comparisons favoured NSAIDs. No clear difference emerged for low-dose ibuprofen against placebo in Makarainen 1986 or MFA against placebo in Muggeridge 1983. Grover 1990 found a difference favouring MFA in women's reported relief of HMB (OR 0.08, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.18), but did not explain how relief was measured. In the unpooled Ylikorkala 1986 cross-over trial, 79% rated naproxen better for HMB reduction and 21% rated placebo better.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Adverse events
document_sections.content: In van Eijkeren 1992, overall adverse-event incidence was comparable between MFA and placebo. Muggeridge 1983 found no change in dysmenorrhoea scores between those treatments. Cross-over comparisons found no difference in overall adverse-event incidence for naproxen or ibuprofen against placebo.

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: No trial contributed meta-analysable evidence for quality of life, TMFL, bleeding days, adherence, acceptability, or resource use and cost in this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 2 NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid
document_sections.content: The review compared blood loss, bleeding duration, quality of life, and treatment acceptability between NSAIDs and tranexamic acid.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective, subjective or both)
document_sections.content: In Bonnar 1996, involving 48 women in the MBL analysis, the tranexamic acid group had 73 mL/cycle less MBL than the MFA group (MD 73 mL/cycle, 95% CI 22 to 124). Women's perceived MBL change did not clearly differ. In the unpooled Andersch 1988 cross-over trial, mean MBL was significantly lower during tranexamic acid cycles (155 mL) than flurbiprofen cycles (223 mL; P < 0.01).

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Number of days' bleeding
document_sections.content: The available study did not establish a clear difference in bleeding duration. The account cites Peto OR 1.44, 95% CI 0.45 to 4.61, for 49 women in 1 study; the document elsewhere assigns that estimate to perceived MBL improvement, while its bleeding-duration summary reports a mean difference.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 Quality of life
document_sections.content: One study involving 49 women found no clear difference in quality-of-life change (Peto OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.27 to 4.73) or treatment acceptability (Peto OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.32 to 4.27). Another study presented outcomes in a form unsuitable for analysis.

document_sections.heading: 2.4 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: No trials supplied meta-analysable results for TMFL, adherence, or resource use and cost; the document also lists acceptability here despite reporting an acceptability analysis above.

document_sections.heading: 3 NSAIDs versus ethamsylate
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996 and Chamberlain 1991 contributed to this treatment comparison.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective, subjective or both)
document_sections.content: Objectively measured MBL showed no established difference immediately after treatment across two studies (MD –42.88 mL/cycle, 95% CI –86.25 to 0.50; 82 women; I2 = 0%) or at six months in one study (MD –70.30 mL/cycle, 95% CI –158.88 to 18.28; 31 women). In one study, participants did not discern a difference in their blood loss (Peto OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.23 to 2.12; 50 women).

document_sections.heading: 3.2 Quality of life
document_sections.content: A single study involving 50 women found no clear quality-of-life difference (Peto OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.18 to 3.72).

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Number of days' bleeding
document_sections.content: Treatment-cycle bleeding days did not clearly differ in one study (MD –0.40 days, 95% CI –1.56 to 0.76; 46 women).

document_sections.heading: 3.4 Patient acceptability of treatment
document_sections.content: More women regarded ethamsylate as unacceptable than regarded NSAIDs as unacceptable (Peto OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.61; 50 women).

document_sections.heading: 3.5 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: The review found no trials suitable for meta-analysis of TMFL, adherence, or resource use and cost. It also lists acceptability among unavailable outcomes here, although an acceptability result is reported in the preceding subsection.

document_sections.heading: 4 NSAIDs versus danazol
document_sections.content: The comparison addresses MBL, quality of life, bleeding days, acceptability, and adverse events.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective)
document_sections.content: Danazol reduced HMB significantly more than NSAIDs (MD 45.06 mL/cycle, 95% CI 18.73 to 71.39; 79 women; 3 studies; I2 = 29%). No trial assessed women's perception of post-treatment MBL.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Quality of life
document_sections.content: Quality of life did not clearly differ between groups in 1 study of 28 women (Peto OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.20 to 7.05).

document_sections.heading: 4.3 Number of days' bleeding
document_sections.content: Menstruation lasted fewer days with danazol than MFA (MD 1.03 days, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.80; 53 women; 2 studies; I2 = 0%).

document_sections.heading: 4.4 Patient acceptability of treatment
document_sections.content: Acceptability did not clearly differ in 1 study involving 40 women (Peto OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.24 to 2.80).

document_sections.heading: 4.5 Adverse events
document_sections.content: In that study, adverse events were less likely with MFA than with danazol (Peto OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.59; 40 women).

document_sections.heading: 4.6 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: No eligible meta-analysis addressed TMFL, adherence, or resource use and cost.

document_sections.heading: 5 NSAIDs versus oral progestogen (luteal phase)
document_sections.content: Two studies assessed MBL and bleeding duration in this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective, subjective or both)
document_sections.content: NSAIDs may have improved MBL compared with oral progestogens (MD –22.97 mL/cycle, 95% CI –46.57 to 0.62; 48 women; 2 studies; I2 = 71%). Differences in participant age and baseline bleeding criteria between studies could explain the substantial heterogeneity.

document_sections.heading: 5.2 Number of days' bleeding
document_sections.content: No clear difference in bleeding duration was established (MD –0.41, 95% CI –0.95 to 0.13; 48 women; 2 studies; I2 = 35%).

document_sections.heading: 5.3 Adverse events
document_sections.content: One study involving 32 women established no clear difference in non-adherence (Peto OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.05 to 14.78), total adverse events (Peto OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.13 to 2.26), headache (Peto OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.14 to 2.86), abdominal pain (Peto OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.15 to 4.96), or nausea (Peto OR 1.79, 95% CI 0.17 to 18.65). Jaisamrarn 2006 supplied no comparative data.

document_sections.heading: 5.4 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: No trial contributed meta-analysable results for TMFL, acceptability, or resource use and cost. The document also lists adherence as unavailable here, despite reporting a non-adherence analysis above.

document_sections.heading: 6 NSAIDs versus progesterone-releasing intrauterine system
document_sections.content: The review distinguishes the older progesterone-releasing IUS from the LNG IUS in interpreting this comparison.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective, subjective or both)
document_sections.content: The comparison against the older progesterone-releasing IUS found no clear difference in HMB reduction (MD –4.00 mL/cycle, 95% CI –31.23 to 23.23; 16 women; 1 study). A separate larger MFA-versus-LNG IUS trial reported highly significant between-group differences in MBL and PBAC scores (P < 0.001 for both), without calculable summary effect measures.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Total menstrual fluid loss
document_sections.content: The MFA-versus-LNG IUS trial also reported a highly significant between-group TMFL difference (P < 0.001), without a calculated summary effect measure.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Number of days' bleeding
document_sections.content: NSAIDs were associated with fewer bleeding days than the older progesterone-releasing IUS, which had been withdrawn from the market since 2001 (MD –5.00 days, 95% CI –6.08 to –3.92; 16 women; 1 study).

document_sections.heading: 6.4 Adverse events
document_sections.content: No clear difference was established for adverse events other than abdominal pain, which may have been less frequent with NSAIDs than with the IUS in 1 study involving 51 women (Peto OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.87).

document_sections.heading: 6.5 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: No trial provided meta-analysable results for quality of life, adherence, acceptability, or resource use and cost.

document_sections.heading: 7 NSAIDs versus oral contraceptive pill
document_sections.content: The review compared objectively assessed MBL between NSAIDs and OCP.

document_sections.heading: 7.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective, subjective or both)
document_sections.content: One study with analysable data did not establish a clear MBL difference (MD 25.25 mL/cycle, 95% CI –22.34 to 72.84; 26 women; 1 study).

document_sections.heading: 7.2 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: No trials provided meta-analysable results for quality of life, TMFL, bleeding days, adherence, acceptability, adverse events, or resource use and cost.

document_sections.heading: 8 Mefenamic acid versus naproxen
document_sections.content: This direct NSAID comparison assessed blood loss, bleeding duration, and adverse events.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective, subjective or both)
document_sections.content: Objectively measured MBL did not clearly differ between mefenamic acid and naproxen (MD 21.00 mL/cycle, 95% CI –5.85 to 47.85; 61 women; 2 studies; I2 = 25%).

document_sections.heading: 8.2 Number of days' bleeding
document_sections.content: Bleeding duration did not clearly differ (MD –0.40 days, 95% CI –1.59 to 0.79; 35 women; 1 study).

document_sections.heading: 8.3 Adverse events
document_sections.content: Overall adverse-event incidence did not clearly differ (Peto OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.00; 35 women; 1 study). Gastrointestinal events were less likely with MFA than naproxen (Peto OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.87; 35 women; 1 study). Central nervous system adverse events showed no clear difference (Peto OR 1.40, 95% CI 0.34 to 5.73; 35 women; 1 study).

document_sections.heading: 8.4 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: The document lists no meta-analysable evidence for quality of life, TMFL, adherence, acceptability, or resource use and cost. It also lists bleeding days here, despite reporting their analysis above.

document_sections.heading: 9 Tranexamic acid plus mefenamic acid versus tranexamic acid
document_sections.content: This comparison examined whether adding MFA to tranexamic acid improved MBL.

document_sections.heading: 9.1 Menstrual blood loss (objective, subjective or both)
document_sections.content: In one study with 55 women, the combined tranexamic acid plus MFA group had a clear reduction from baseline in PBAC score, from 246 to 100 at 6 months' follow-up (P < 0.01). Within the tranexamic acid-only group, PBAC changed from 250 at baseline to 125 at 6 months' follow-up without a clearly established change (P > 0.05). These within-group tests do not provide an analysed between-group effect.

document_sections.heading: 9.2 Other outcomes
document_sections.content: No trials supplied meta-analysable results for quality of life, TMFL, bleeding days, adherence, acceptability, adverse events, or resource use and cost.

document_sections.heading: D I S C U S S I O N Summary of main results
document_sections.content: The authors interpret comparative effectiveness and safety alongside the limited quantity and quality of the evidence.

document_sections.heading: NSAIDs versus placebo
document_sections.content: The meta-analysed trial and five of six cross-over studies supported greater MBL reduction with NSAIDs than placebo. The single pooled trial had important limitations: 42% of randomised participants dropped out and analysis was not by intention to treat. Another study found a highly significant patient-perceived difference in relief from HMB favouring NSAIDs.

document_sections.heading: NSAIDs versus other medical treatments
document_sections.content: Both tranexamic acid and danazol reduced MBL more than the NSAIDs studied. An unpooled cross-over trial supported the tranexamic acid comparison. For danazol, two studies supported a clear difference, but the third, Cameron 1987, had a significantly higher pretreatment MBL in the danazol group—almost double—and requires caution. Limited direct comparisons did not suggest different efficacy among NSAIDs, supporting their combination in other comparisons.

document_sections.heading: Tranexamic acid plus NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid alone
document_sections.content: Authors of one trial reported a significant baseline-to-follow-up PBAC reduction after six months of combined tranexamic acid and NSAID treatment, but not after tranexamic acid alone. The form of the data prevented inclusion in the analysis.

document_sections.heading: Overall comparisons
document_sections.content: No clear MBL reduction difference was established between NSAIDs and ethamsylate, luteal-phase oral progestogen, the older progesterone-releasing IUS, or OCP. Despite limited data, NSAIDs appeared more effective than placebo and less effective than tranexamic acid, danazol, or LNG IUS. Adverse events occurred more often with danazol than NSAIDs, and randomised evidence on NSAID-related costs or resource use was unavailable. The older-IUS comparison was very small and potentially affected by baseline imbalance; that system was withdrawn in 2001. In Reid 2005, a newer system delivering 20 g of levonorgestrel daily reduced MBL and TMFL more effectively. Cited evidence indicates that blood accounts for only a third of TMFL in women with normal menses. The authors therefore discuss whether total fluid volume, rather than blood alone, drives care-seeking. Reid 2005 reported strong correlations between MBL and TMFL and proposed TMFL as an easier-to-measure estimate; whether women prioritise menstrual-loss volume over composition remains to be tested.

document_sections.heading: Overall completeness and applicability of evidence
document_sections.content: MBL varies across cycles, complicating assessment. Haynes 1977 reported greater cycle-to-cycle variation among women with HMB (39 mL to 271 mL) than among women with normal periods. The discussion describes inclusion of objectively measured MBL greater than 80 mL/cycle for two or more pretreatment cycles, alongside studies enrolling women with a subjective HMB complaint; the methods section instead specifies one or more cycles. Alkaline haematin is the standard objective measure, but women's own perception is also a valid treatment-effect measure. Cited research indicates that many care-seeking women have normal measured MBL, and Fraser 1981 suggested little treatment response below 35 mL. Inclusion of some women without objectively excessive MBL may therefore have underestimated treatment–placebo differences. Danazol shortened bleeding relative to NSAIDs; bleeding lasted longer with the older progesterone-releasing IUS, although that finding came from only one small trial. Bleeding days were not compared with OCP. Stewart 2001 reported that abdominal pain was more likely with LNG IUS than MFA up to six months but generally subsided over time. Overall adverse events were more frequent with danazol. Although refusal to continue was similar—50% with danazol versus 47% with MFA—about 80% of danazol-group refusers cited adverse effects, while 100% of MFA-group refusers cited inadequate efficacy. Ethamsylate was considered unacceptable more often than MFA. Included trials generally examined two or three treated cycles; one study assessed one month after withdrawal. An observational study, Fraser 1983, followed 34 women receiving MFA over a 16-month period and reported sustained MBL reductions of 25% to 35% and improved quality of life; this is not longer-term randomised evidence. Trials also did not examine some treatment schedules. The authors state that longer oral progestogen dosing, from days five to 26 of the cycle, and longer treatment across multiple cycles are needed to assess these comparisons adequately.

document_sections.heading: Comparison of individual NSAIDs
document_sections.content: Randomised studies have not thoroughly explored clinical differences between NSAIDs. Two included studies found no difference between MFA and naproxen in post-treatment MBL or overall adverse events. MFA was associated with fewer gastrointestinal effects, but this finding came from only one small trial.

document_sections.heading: Quality of the evidence
document_sections.content: Although 19 trials were eligible, all were small and underpowered, and many outcomes depended on a single trial. Two of the nine meta-analysed trials, Cameron 1987 and Hall 1987, reported skewed MBL outcomes appropriately as medians and ranges. Treating medians as means and estimating SD enabled pooling; sensitivity analysis excluding Cameron 1987 did not change conclusions. Hall 1987 was the only post-treatment MBL comparison between MFA and naproxen, and its Mann-Whitney U test agreed with the meta-analysis that no clear difference was established. Cameron 1987 and Chamberlain 1991 had baseline imbalances, but sensitivity analyses found that including them did not substantially change results. Fraser 1981 investigated carryover in its MFA–placebo cross-over trial: placebo-cycle blood loss was nonsignificantly greater when MFA came first, while MFA-cycle blood loss was significantly lower when placebo came first (P < 0.01). The small suggested carryover did not reach significance. Hall 1987 found no carryover (P = 0.96). Because MBL is generally believed to return rapidly to baseline after medical therapy stops, the authors judged substantial carryover effects on cross-over results unlikely.

document_sections.heading: Potential biases in the review process
document_sections.content: The extensive search reduced the likelihood of publication bias but could not exclude it; too few studies made funnel-plot analysis meaningful. The authors judged their study-selection, extraction, and quality-assessment procedures appropriate for limiting reviewer error and bias.

document_sections.heading: Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews
document_sections.content: The search found no other systematic reviews of NSAIDs. The authors report that NICE 2007 guidance recommends NSAIDs alongside tranexamic acid and OCPs as a second-line option when either hormonal or non-hormonal therapy is acceptable. When hormonal therapy is unacceptable, that guidance places NSAIDs alongside tranexamic acid as a first-line option. These are recommendations attributed to the cited guidance.

document_sections.heading: A U T H O R S ' C O N C L U S I O N S Implications for practice
document_sections.content: The review offers limited evidence that NSAIDs, especially the frequently studied MFA, reduce HMB. Danazol, tranexamic acid, and LNG IUS are more effective. Other medical treatments appear similarly effective to NSAIDs, although MFA may be more effective than ethamsylate or oral progestogen. Danazol shortens menstruation but causes adverse events more often than NSAIDs. Gastrointestinal effects appear less frequent with MFA than naproxen. Demonstrated NSAID benefits are modest, and some women retain objectively defined menorrhagia after treatment. A convincing history of heavy bleeding does not always coincide with excess MBL measured by alkaline haematin; blood-loss-reducing treatments are unlikely to work as well when measured loss is not excessive. Optimal treatment assessment must consider not only efficacy but also cost, convenience, and beneficial and adverse effects on symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Implications for research
document_sections.content: Further RCTs comparing individual NSAIDs are needed to identify an optimal option because MFA dominates the existing evidence. Many analyses relied on only one RCT, leaving comparisons involving dysmenorrhoea, adherence, acceptability, and adverse events inadequately assessed. Nevertheless, because several other medical treatments appear more effective than NSAIDs, additional RCTs are unlikely to substantially change the review's overall findings. Future HMB treatment comparisons should assess longer treatment over several cycles and oral progestogen administered during three of the four weeks of a cycle. Adequately designed trials should also investigate whether adding NSAIDs to other medical treatments improves efficacy.

document_sections.heading: Characteristics of included studies [ordered by study ID]
document_sections.content: The study profiles describe participants, designs, interventions, outcomes and risk-of-bias judgments for the included trials.

document_sections.heading: Andersch 1988
document_sections.content: This Swedish cross-over trial compared flurbiprofen with tranexamic acid for menstrual blood loss, bleeding duration and adverse events. Randomisation and allocation concealment were unclear, and treatment was not blinded. Outcomes from the first treatment period were unavailable, preventing inclusion in the pooled analysis; results for bleeding duration and adverse events were also unavailable.

document_sections.heading: Bonnar 1996
document_sections.content: This Irish parallel-group trial compared MFA, ethamsylate and tranexamic acid in women with objectively heavy menstrual bleeding. It assessed menstrual blood loss, bleeding duration, perceived blood loss, dysmenorrhoea, adverse events and willingness to continue treatment. A computer-generated list determined randomisation, but allocation concealment was unspecified and treatment was not blinded. Withdrawals occurred during treatment; the study profile gives inconsistent descriptions of whether analysis followed intention to treat.

document_sections.heading: Cameron 1987
document_sections.content: This UK trial allocated women to MFA, danazol, norethisterone or a progesterone coil and measured menstrual blood loss. The randomisation method was unspecified, treatment was unblinded, and the danazol group had significantly higher pretreatment blood loss than the other groups.

document_sections.heading: Cameron 1990
document_sections.content: This UK comparison of MFA and norethisterone assessed menstrual blood loss, bleeding days, adverse events and adherence. Women were screened for ovulatory cycles and objectively heavy bleeding before randomisation. The randomisation method was unspecified, treatment was unblinded, and the groups were comparable at baseline.

document_sections.heading: Chamberlain 1991
document_sections.content: This UK double-blind, parallel-group trial compared MFA with ethamsylate during treatment and after withdrawal. Postrandomisation exclusions prevented an intention-to-treat analysis. The groups differed in pretreatment blood loss. The review analysed unpublished data from the same study because detailed published data were unavailable, although group numbers differed between the two sources; adverse-event data were unavailable from the unpublished data.

document_sections.heading: Dockeray 1989
document_sections.content: This unblinded Irish trial compared MFA with danazol after untreated control cycles. It assessed menstrual blood loss, bleeding days, dysmenorrhoea, adverse events and willingness to continue treatment. The groups were comparable at baseline. A woman receiving MFA was withdrawn because of adverse effects, and the analysis was not intention to treat.

document_sections.heading: Fraser 1981
document_sections.content: This Australian double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over trial evaluated MFA in women with varied causes of menorrhagia. The review used only the subgroup with ovulatory menorrhagia. Withdrawal and the absence of an intention-to-treat analysis raised attrition concerns. First-period results were unavailable, so the subgroup's results could not be pooled.

document_sections.heading: Fraser 1991
document_sections.content: This Australian, unblinded cross-over trial compared MFA in random order with naproxen, an oral contraceptive or danazol, using untreated cycles between treatment periods. It measured menstrual blood loss. Loss to follow-up occurred without an intention-to-treat analysis; the author supplied results from the first treatment period.

document_sections.heading: Grover 1990
document_sections.content: This Indian double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel-group trial compared MFA with placebo in women reporting menorrhagia. Its outcomes were perceived relief and bleeding duration. The randomisation method and the way relief was measured were unspecified, and placebo-group bleeding-duration data were unavailable.

document_sections.heading: Hall 1987
document_sections.content: This UK double-blind cross-over trial compared MFA with naproxen for menstrual blood loss, bleeding duration, dysmenorrhoea and adverse events. Exclusions and withdrawals after randomisation, without an intention-to-treat analysis, produced high attrition risk. The authors found no significant carryover effect; first-period menstrual blood loss data were available.

document_sections.heading: Jaisamrarn 2006
document_sections.content: This Thai randomised trial listed tranexamic acid, norethisterone and MFA as treatments, with PBAC and quality of life as outcomes. Results and numbers assigned to each group were unavailable. Randomisation, allocation concealment, blinding and incomplete-outcome risk remained unclear.

document_sections.heading: Makarainen 1986
document_sections.content: This Finnish double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over study compared ibuprofen regimens with placebo in a subgroup with primary menorrhagia. It assessed menstrual blood loss, adverse events, bleeding duration and menstrual pain. First-period data were unavailable for pooling, as were results for bleeding duration and pain.

document_sections.heading: Muggeridge 1983
document_sections.content: This UK double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over trial examined MFA, menstrual blood loss, dysmenorrhoea and adverse events. Follow-up losses occurred without an intention-to-treat analysis. First-period and adverse-event data were unavailable.

document_sections.heading: Najam 2010
document_sections.content: This Indian single-centre, single-blinded parallel-group trial compared tranexamic acid plus MFA with tranexamic acid alone and assessed haemoglobin and PBAC. Its authors analysed change from baseline separately within each randomised group rather than making an appropriate between-group comparison. Numbers analysed and withdrawal details were not reported.

document_sections.heading: Reid 2005
document_sections.content: This UK, single-centre, unblinded parallel-group trial compared MFA with LNG IUS in women with objectively confirmed idiopathic menorrhagia. It used computer-generated randomisation and concealed allocation, with an intention-to-treat analysis. Discontinuations attributed to MFA included non-adherence, diarrhoea and inadequate effect; those attributed to LNG IUS involved partial or complete expulsion.

document_sections.heading: Rybo 1981
document_sections.content: This Swedish double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over study compared naproxen with placebo. The review used the subgroup with primary menorrhagia rather than participants with IUD-induced bleeding. First-period data were unavailable for pooling.

document_sections.heading: Tsang 1987
document_sections.content: This Canadian double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over study compared MFA with placebo for objectively measured menstrual blood loss. Follow-up losses occurred without an intention-to-treat analysis, and first-period data were unavailable for pooling.

document_sections.heading: van Eijkeren 1992
document_sections.content: This Dutch double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel-group trial assessed MFA for menstrual blood loss and adverse events. Allocation concealment was judged adequate. Withdrawals were substantial and there was no intention-to-treat analysis; results were reported only for women who subsequently underwent hysterectomy. A participant discontinued MFA because of rash and itching.

document_sections.heading: Ylikorkala 1986
document_sections.content: This Finnish double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over trial assessed naproxen for menstrual blood loss, perceived improvement and adverse events. First-period data were unavailable for pooling.

document_sections.heading: Characteristics of excluded studies [ordered by study ID]
document_sections.content: The table identifies excluded trials and their reasons for exclusion. Famuyide 2017 and Gupta 2013 allowed participants to choose the medical treatment rather than randomising them specifically to NSAIDs. Martinez Alcala 1979 measured bleeding through sanitary-pad use, which did not reliably correspond to objective menstrual blood loss. Naafe 2018 compared mefenamic acid with mefenamic acid plus herbal medicine. Vargyas 1987 included participants with intrauterine devices, an iatrogenic cause of heavy bleeding, without separately available results for the others.

document_sections.heading: Characteristics of ongoing studies [ordered by study ID]
document_sections.content: The profile for NCT02943655 describes a randomised parallel-group trial of a combined contraceptive pill, Medroxyprogesterone acetate and Mefenamic acid for heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding without an organic cause. Its specified outcome is menstrual blood loss at 3 months.

document_sections.heading: DATA AND ANALYSES
document_sections.content: The analyses organise the included studies by treatment comparison and outcome. Pooled results and findings that could not be pooled are presented separately.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 1. NSAIDs versus placebo
document_sections.content: The comparison covers menstrual blood loss, lack of perceived improvement and adverse events. It also identifies cross-over results reported descriptively rather than pooled.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 1.1. Comparison 1 NSAIDs versus placebo, Outcome 1 Menstrual blood loss (MBL) (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: The table compares post-treatment menstrual blood loss with mefenamic acid and placebo in van Eijkeren 1992; its estimated difference favours mefenamic acid.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 1.2. Comparison 1 NSAIDs versus placebo, Outcome 2 Proportion with no subjective improvement in MBL.
document_sections.content: The table presents Grover 1990's comparison of women reporting no subjective improvement with mefenamic acid or placebo; the result favours mefenamic acid.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 1.3. Comparison 1 NSAIDs versus placebo, Outcome 3 Adverse events.
document_sections.content: The table compares adverse-event occurrence with mefenamic acid and placebo in van Eijkeren 1992, without a clear difference.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 1.4. Comparison 1 NSAIDs versus placebo, Outcome 4 MBL and other outcomes (descriptive results).
document_sections.content: The descriptive table presents cross-over findings for mefenamic acid, naproxen and ibuprofen against placebo. Most reported comparisons favour the active NSAID for menstrual blood loss, but Muggeridge 1983 found no significant difference for mefenamic acid. That study also found no significant difference in dysmenorrhoea scores. Adverse-event proportions are shown where available.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 2. NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid
document_sections.content: The comparison addresses menstrual blood loss, perceived improvement, bleeding duration, dysmenorrhoea or quality of life, treatment acceptability and descriptive results.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 2.1. Comparison 2 NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid, Outcome 1 Menstrual blood loss (MBL) (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996's results show greater menstrual blood loss with the NSAID than with tranexamic acid.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 2.2. Comparison 2 NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid, Outcome 2 Proportion with no subjective improvement in MBL.
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996's results do not establish a difference between the treatments in perceived lack of improvement.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 2.3. Comparison 2 NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid, Outcome 3 Number of days' bleeding.
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996's results do not establish a difference in bleeding duration between treatment groups.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 2.4. Comparison 2 NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid, Outcome 4 Proportion with no improvement in quality of life or dysmenorrhoea (or both).
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996's results do not establish a difference in the proportion without improvement in quality of life or dysmenorrhoea.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 2.5. Comparison 2 NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid, Outcome 5 Proportion who found treatment unacceptable.
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996's results do not establish a difference in treatment unacceptability.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 2.6. Comparison 2 NSAIDs versus tranexamic acid, Outcome 6 MBL and other outcomes (descriptive results).
document_sections.content: Andersch 1988 reports significantly less menstrual blood loss during tranexamic acid cycles than during flurbiprofen cycles. The table also gives adverse-event proportions, but their difference was not tested.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 3. NSAIDs versus ethamsylate
document_sections.content: The comparison covers menstrual blood loss during and after treatment, perceived improvement, dysmenorrhoea or quality of life, bleeding duration and treatment acceptability.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 3.1. Comparison 3 NSAIDs versus ethamsylate, Outcome 1 Menstrual blood loss a er treatment (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: The pooled estimate from Bonnar 1996 and Chamberlain 1991 trends towards less menstrual blood loss with NSAIDs, but the review does not establish a clear difference.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 3.2. Comparison 3 NSAIDs versus ethamsylate, Outcome 2 Menstrual blood loss 1–6 months a er treatment (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: Chamberlain 1991's post-treatment follow-up results do not establish a difference in menstrual blood loss.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 3.3. Comparison 3 NSAIDs versus ethamsylate, Outcome 3 Proportion with no subjective improvement in MBL.
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996's results do not establish a difference in perceived lack of improvement.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 3.4. Comparison 3 NSAIDs versus ethamsylate, Outcome 4 Proportion with no improvement in quality of life or dysmenorrhoea (or both).
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996's results do not establish a difference in lack of improvement in quality of life or dysmenorrhoea.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 3.5. Comparison 3 NSAIDs versus ethamsylate, Outcome 5 Number of days' bleeding.
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996's results do not establish a difference in bleeding duration.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 3.6. Comparison 3 NSAIDs versus ethamsylate, Outcome 6 Proportion who found treatment unacceptable.
document_sections.content: Bonnar 1996 shows that treatment was considered unacceptable less often with the NSAID than with ethamsylate.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 4. NSAIDs versus danazol
document_sections.content: The comparison covers menstrual blood loss, dysmenorrhoea or quality of life, bleeding duration, acceptability and adverse events.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 4.1. Comparison 4 NSAIDs versus danazol, Outcome 1 Menstrual blood loss (MBL) (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: The pooled findings from Cameron 1987, Dockeray 1989 and Fraser 1991 favour danazol for reducing menstrual blood loss. Cameron 1987 had unequal pretreatment blood loss between groups.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 4.2. Comparison 4 NSAIDs versus danazol, Outcome 2 Proportion with no improvement in quality of life or dysmenorrhoea (or both).
document_sections.content: Dockeray 1989's results do not establish a difference in lack of improvement in quality of life or dysmenorrhoea.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 4.3. Comparison 4 NSAIDs versus danazol, Outcome 3 Number of days' bleeding.
document_sections.content: The combined results from Cameron 1987 and Dockeray 1989 favour danazol for shorter menstrual bleeding.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 4.4. Comparison 4 NSAIDs versus danazol, Outcome 4 Proportion who found treatment unacceptable.
document_sections.content: Dockeray 1989's results do not establish a difference in treatment unacceptability.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 4.5. Comparison 4 NSAIDs versus danazol, Outcome 5 Adverse events.
document_sections.content: Dockeray 1989 reports fewer adverse events with the NSAID than with danazol.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 5. NSAIDs versus oral progestogens
document_sections.content: The comparison addresses menstrual blood loss, bleeding duration, non-adherence, total adverse events, headache, abdominal pain and nausea.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 5.1. Comparison 5 NSAIDs versus oral progestogens, Outcome 1 Menstrual blood loss (MBL) (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: The combined findings from Cameron 1987 and Cameron 1990 suggest that NSAIDs may reduce menstrual blood loss more than oral progestogens, but do not establish a clear difference. Heterogeneity was substantial.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 5.2. Comparison 5 NSAIDs versus oral progestogens, Outcome 2 Number of days' bleeding.
document_sections.content: The pooled comparison does not establish a difference in bleeding duration. The document presents conflicting individual-study entries for this outcome; its pooled estimate is unchanged across those presentations.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 5.3. Comparison 5 NSAIDs versus oral progestogens, Outcome 3 Proportion with non-adherence.
document_sections.content: Cameron 1990's results do not establish a difference in non-adherence.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 5.4. Comparison 5 NSAIDs versus oral progestogens, Outcome 4 Total adverse events.
document_sections.content: Cameron 1990's results do not establish a difference in overall adverse events.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 5.5. Comparison 5 NSAIDs versus oral progestogens, Outcome 5 Adverse events – headache.
document_sections.content: Cameron 1990's results do not establish a difference in headache.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 5.6. Comparison 5 NSAIDs versus oral progestogens, Outcome 6 Adverse events – abdominal pain.
document_sections.content: Cameron 1990's results do not establish a difference in abdominal pain.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 5.7. Comparison 5 NSAIDs versus oral progestogens, Outcome 7 Adverse events – nausea.
document_sections.content: Cameron 1990's results do not establish a difference in nausea.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 6. NSAIDs versus progesterone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS)
document_sections.content: The comparison covers menstrual blood loss, descriptive results, bleeding duration and specific adverse events. Its analyses include the older progesterone-releasing system and a separate trial of LNG IUS.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 6.1. Comparison 6 NSAIDs versus progesterone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS), Outcome 1 Menstrual blood loss (MBL) (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: Cameron 1987's comparison with the progesterone-releasing system does not establish a difference in menstrual blood loss.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 6.2. Comparison 6 NSAIDs versus progesterone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS), Outcome 2 MBL and other outcomes (descriptive results).
document_sections.content: Reid 2005's descriptive results compare NSAIDs with LNG IUS for menstrual blood loss, total menstrual fluid loss and PBAC at follow-up. All reported comparisons favour LNG IUS, but the results were not combined into summary effect estimates.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 6.3. Comparison 6 NSAIDs versus progesterone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS), Outcome 3 Number of days' bleeding.
document_sections.content: Cameron 1987 reports fewer bleeding days with the NSAID than with the older progesterone-releasing system.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 6.4. Comparison 6 NSAIDs versus progesteronereleasing intrauterine system (IUS), Outcome 4 Adverse events.
document_sections.content: Reid 2005 compares specific adverse events between NSAIDs and LNG IUS. Abdominal pain was less frequent in the NSAID group; the analyses do not establish clear differences for headache, ovarian cyst, breast pain, nausea, diarrhoea or upper respiratory infection.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 7. NSAIDs versus oral contraceptive pill (OCP)
document_sections.content: This comparison assesses menstrual blood loss.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 7.1. Comparison 7 NSAIDs versus oral contraceptive pill (OCP), Outcome 1 Menstrual blood loss (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: Fraser 1991's results do not establish a difference in menstrual blood loss between NSAIDs and OCP.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 8. Mefenamic acid versus naproxen
document_sections.content: This comparison assesses menstrual blood loss, bleeding duration, total adverse events, gastrointestinal adverse events and central nervous system adverse events.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 8.1. Comparison 8 Mefenamic acid versus naproxen, Outcome 1 Menstrual blood loss (mL/cycle).
document_sections.content: The combined results from Fraser 1991 and Hall 1987 do not establish a difference in menstrual blood loss between mefenamic acid and naproxen.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 8.2. Comparison 8 Mefenamic acid versus naproxen, Outcome 2 Number of days' bleeding.
document_sections.content: Hall 1987's results do not establish a difference in bleeding duration.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 8.3. Comparison 8 Mefenamic acid versus naproxen, Outcome 3 Total adverse events.
document_sections.content: Hall 1987's results do not establish a difference in total adverse events.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 8.4. Comparison 8 Mefenamic acid versus naproxen, Outcome 4 Gastrointestinal adverse events.
document_sections.content: Hall 1987 reports fewer gastrointestinal adverse events with mefenamic acid than with naproxen.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 8.5. Comparison 8 Mefenamic acid versus naproxen, Outcome 5 Central nervous system adverse events.
document_sections.content: Hall 1987's results do not establish a difference in central nervous system adverse events.

document_sections.heading: Comparison 9. Tranexamic acid and mefenamic acid versus tranexamic acid
document_sections.content: This comparison presents PBAC follow-up results descriptively because the data were unsuitable for a pooled between-group effect estimate.

document_sections.heading: Analysis 9.1. Comparison 9 Tranexamic acid and mefenamic acid versus tranexamic acid, Outcome 1 Pictorial blood loss assessment chart (PBAC) score at 6 months' follow-up.
document_sections.content: Najam 2010 reports a significant within-group reduction in PBAC from baseline with tranexamic acid plus mefenamic acid, but not with tranexamic acid alone. These separate within-group tests do not establish a treatment difference between the randomised groups.

document_sections.heading: APPENDICES
document_sections.content: The appendices document the database-specific strategies used to identify studies of heavy menstrual bleeding and NSAIDs.

document_sections.heading: Appendix 1. Gynaecology and Fertility Group specialised register search strategy
document_sections.content: The specialised-register search combined terms for heavy or abnormal menstrual bleeding with terms for NSAIDs and individual agents. It used the PROCITE platform and was searched on 1 April 2019.

document_sections.heading: Appendix 2. Cochrane Central Register of Studies Online (CRSO) search strategy
document_sections.content: The CENTRAL CRSO strategy combined subject headings and text terms for menstrual disorders with those for NSAIDs and cyclooxygenase inhibitors. It used the web platform and was searched on 1 April 2019.

document_sections.heading: Appendix 3. MEDLINE search strategy
document_sections.content: The MEDLINE strategy combined menstrual-bleeding and anti-inflammatory-drug terms with a randomised-trial search filter, excluding animal-only records. It searched the OVID platform from 1946 to 1 April 2019.

document_sections.heading: Appendix 4. Embase search strategy
document_sections.content: The Embase strategy combined menstrual-disorder and anti-inflammatory-drug terms with clinical-trial terms while excluding designated case-study, case-report, abstract-report and letter records. It searched OVID from 1980 to 1 April 2019.

document_sections.heading: Appendix 5. PsycINFO search strategy
document_sections.content: The PsycINFO strategy combined anti-inflammatory-drug and menstrual-disorder terms with treatment and trial-related terms. It searched OVID from 1806 to 1 April 2019.

document_sections.heading: WHAT'S NEW
document_sections.content: The update table records that the 3 April 2019 search yielded no new data that changed the conclusions. It records inclusion of Jaisamrarn 2006 without analysable data, exclusion of Famuyide 2017 and Gupta 2013, and identification of the ongoing NCT02943655 trial.

document_sections.heading: HISTORY
document_sections.content: The history table records changes to eligibility criteria and newly identified studies in earlier updates. The 31 July 2012 update added a study and expanded eligibility to combined NSAID and tranexamic acid treatment without changing conclusions. The 17 July 2007 update involved a substantive change and revised conclusions.

document_sections.heading: DIFFERENCES BETWEEN PROTOCOL AND REVIEW
document_sections.content: In the 2012 update, eligibility was expanded to permit comparisons of NSAIDs combined with other medical treatments against other medical treatments.

document_sections.heading: NOTES
document_sections.content: The September and October 2001 search found no newly eligible trial. The April 2007 update included one published trial and left one abstract awaiting assessment. The July 2012 update included one published RCT. The 2019 search found no new eligible trials.
